extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of early-modern epistemology/philosophy (e.g., readers of Locke)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for judging when ideas (simple, complex, modes, substances) can be called true/false or right/wrong, and guidance on the association of ideas and its effects on reasoning and education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and Falsehood properly belong to Propositions, not to Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth and falsehood properly belong to PROPOSITIONS: IDEAS, being bare appearances or perceptions in the mind, cannot properly and simply in themselves be said to be true or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ideas are called true/false there is usually a tacit or secret proposition (an affirmation or negation) underpinning that denomination; the mind must pass a judgment on ideas before they can be so termed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas are called true/false only when referred by the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas in themselves, as mere perceptions or appearances, are neither true nor false; they become so only when the mind refers them (makes a tacit supposition or judgment) to something extraneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common occasions where this happens include referring an idea to other men's ideas, to real existence, or to supposed real essences. Without such reference (i.e., without an affirmation/negation) the idea alone is not true or false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to Other Men’s Ideas (conformity to common names)
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea may be judged true or false when the mind supposes it conformable to the idea in OTHER MEN’S MINDS called by the same common name (e.g., ideas of justice, temperance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the most usual sense of falsehood for mixed modes: a person's idea is 'false' in this sense when it differs from the ideas commonly signified by the name among others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to Real Existence (conformity to things that exist)
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea may be called true or false when the mind supposes it conformable to some REAL EXISTENCE; e.g., the idea of a man (true) vs the idea of a centaur (false) as representations of existing substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex ideas of substances that do not conform to any real beings are false in this respect. This criterion compares the idea against the existence of things outside the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to real Constitution or Essence
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas may be judged in reference to 'that REAL constitution and ESSENCE of anything, whereon all its properties depend'; ideas that fail to conform to the real essence are false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most of our ideas of substances are false under this standard because they do not capture the unknown internal constitution (essence) from which many properties flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas of modes and relations are originals and adequate
rubrics_metrics.description: COMPLEX ideas of MODES AND RELATIONS are originals, archetypes, not copies: they are collections the mind itself puts together and thus 'cannot but be adequate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because these complex ideas are constructed by the mind to contain precisely what the mind intends, they are deemed adequate and not the kinds of ideas liable to the falsity that applies to ideas of substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple ideas are least liable to be false
rubrics_metrics.description: SIMPLE IDEAS are least liable to be mistaken when judged against other people's ideas because they are few, sensory, and easily rectified by observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names of simple ideas (e.g., colours, tastes) are rarely misapplied, and a person can usually use the senses or everyday observation to confirm and correct them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas, especially mixed modes, are most liable to be false (in relation to others’ ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: COMPLEX IDEAS are much more liable to be false when judged by conformity to the ideas of others; MIXED MODES are particularly vulnerable because their components and boundaries are constructed by people and lack a single sensible standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is harder to determine whether actions or character traits (justice, liberality) fall under a given mixed-mode name, so disagreement across minds is common and leads to judgments of falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple ideas cannot be false with respect to real existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple ideas, being perceptions produced by powers in external objects, are just the appearances they are and therefore 'cannot be false' as representations of those powers producing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if different people's organs produced slightly different appearances, as long as each person's perceptions reliably distinguish objects for use and communication, the simple ideas function as true marks of distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of substances may be false with respect to existing things
rubrics_metrics.description: Our complex ideas of substances may be false when referred to patterns in things themselves; such falsehood arises when the complex idea does not match how simple ideas are united in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three principal ways this falsity occurs: (1) joining simple ideas that nature never unites (e.g., horse that barks), (2) separating a simple idea that is always joined with others (direct negation), and (3) omitting inseparable simple ideas so the idea is inadequate rather than strictly false. Additionally, judging a complex idea to be the real essence when it is only a small subset of properties is a greater mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth or Falsehood always supposes Affirmation or Negation (propositional standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth or falsehood depends on some judgment—an affirmation or negation—where signs (ideas or words) are joined or separated according to whether the things they stand for agree or disagree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus truth lies in propositions (how signs are combined), not in bare ideas; falsehood is the contrary arrangement that disagrees with the actual relations among the things represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas are more properly called Right or Wrong in relation to names or reality
rubrics_metrics.description: When considered by the mind in reference to proper signification of names or to reality, ideas may fitly be called RIGHT or WRONG rather than true/false, since truth/falsehood properly belong to propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This terminological advice recommends speaking of ideas as right/wrong according to their agreement with patterns or uses, reserving truth/falsehood for judgmental (propositional) contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong connexion (association) of ideas causes unreasonableness and error
rubrics_metrics.description: Irregular or accidental associations of ideas (formed by chance or custom) unite ideas not allied by nature and produce unreasonable opinions, passions, and actions in people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such associations become strong habits (intellectual and moral), often indistinguishable from what appears natural, and are a major source of error, prejudice, antipathies, and irrational behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom forms habitual associations—educators should prevent undue connections in children
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom settles trains of thinking and the mind makes associations by repeated conjunction; young people are most susceptible and those educating children should watch and prevent undue connexions of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: because early accidental pairings of ideas can last a lifetime (e.g., aversion to reading due to punishment), careful education should avoid creating harmful or irrelevant associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some associations resist reason and require time/disuse to cure
rubrics_metrics.description: Once strong associations are settled, reason alone often cannot dissolve them; time and disuse (separation of representations) are sometimes necessary to remove the joined ideas' effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: grief persisting despite rational consolation, phobias tied to places or objects; clinical or pedagogical interventions should account for the power of habit and the potential need for non-rational remedies (time, gradual separation).
